cues.text: Look at these two molecules. Carbon dioxide has three atoms. Water has three atoms too.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Look at these two molecules. Carbon dioxide has three atoms. Water has three atoms too.

cues.text: We can draw both as straight lines on paper. But a Lewis drawing need not show the real shape.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] We can draw both as straight lines on paper. But a Lewis drawing need not show the real shape.

cues.text: But lift them off the page, into three dimensions, and something changes.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [curious] But lift them off the page, into three dimensions, and something changes.

cues.text: Carbon dioxide stays perfectly straight. One hundred and eighty degrees.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Carbon dioxide stays perfectly straight. One hundred and eighty degrees.

cues.text: Water bends, to an angle of about one hundred and four point five degrees.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Water bends, to an angle of about one hundred and four point five degrees.

cues.text: Why? Why don't water's atoms simply line up? These shapes are not random.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [short pause] [curious] Why? Why don't water's atoms simply line up? These shapes are not random.

cues.text: The answer is hidden in electrons we cannot see. This is molecular geometry, explained visually.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [warmly] The answer is hidden in electrons we cannot see. This is molecular geometry, explained visually.

cues.text: Last time, we discovered why atoms bond at all. Sharing electrons lowers the energy, and overlapping orbitals make sigma and pi bonds.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Last time, we discovered why atoms bond at all. Sharing electrons lowers the energy, and overlapping orbitals make sigma and pi bonds.

cues.text: We drew those bonds with Lewis structures: letters for atoms, lines for shared pairs, dots for lone pairs.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] We drew those bonds with Lewis structures: letters for atoms, lines for shared pairs, dots for lone pairs.

cues.text: Here is methane. One carbon, four hydrogens, four single bonds, drawn as a neat flat cross.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Here is methane. One carbon, four hydrogens, four single bonds, drawn as a neat flat cross.

cues.text: A Lewis structure is excellent bookkeeping. It tells us which atoms are connected, and where the electron pairs are counted.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] A Lewis structure is excellent bookkeeping. It tells us which atoms are connected, and where the electron pairs are counted.

cues.text: But it is drawn on flat paper. So is methane really flat, with its bonds ninety degrees apart?
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [curious] But it is drawn on flat paper. So is methane really flat, with its bonds ninety degrees apart?

cues.text: Turn the flat version on its side, and it collapses into a line. Every bond is squeezed into one plane.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Turn the flat version on its side, and it collapses into a line. Every bond is squeezed into one plane.

cues.text: The real molecule does something smarter. The four bonds lift out of the plane and spread through all three dimensions.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [warmly] The real molecule does something smarter. The four bonds lift out of the plane and spread through all three dimensions.

cues.text: They point to the corners of a tetrahedron, about one hundred and nine point five degrees apart. Wider than ninety.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] They point to the corners of a tetrahedron, about one hundred and nine point five degrees apart. Wider than ninety.

cues.text: So the Lewis structure tells us the connections. It doesn't tell us the shape.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] So the Lewis structure tells us the connections. It doesn't tell us the shape.

cues.text: To predict shape, we need to think about the space that electrons occupy around an atom.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [short pause] [thoughtful] To predict shape, we need to think about the space that electrons occupy around an atom.

cues.text: Picture a central atom, surrounded by regions of electron density. A bond is one region. A lone pair is another.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Picture a central atom, surrounded by regions of electron density. A bond is one region. A lone pair is another.

cues.text: Each region is rich in electrons, so in this simple picture, the regions repel one another. Push two of them together, and watch.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Each region is rich in electrons, so in this simple picture, the regions repel one another. Push two of them together, and watch.

cues.text: They spread apart until they sit on opposite sides, straight through the atom. One hundred and eighty degrees.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [thoughtful] They spread apart until they sit on opposite sides, straight through the atom. One hundred and eighty degrees.

cues.text: Add a third region. The three push each other around until they share the circle equally.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Add a third region. The three push each other around until they share the circle equally.

cues.text: One hundred and twenty degrees apart, all in one flat plane.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] One hundred and twenty degrees apart, all in one flat plane.

cues.text: Now a fourth. Lay the triangle flat, and drop the new region on top.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Now a fourth. Lay the triangle flat, and drop the new region on top.

cues.text: The three below fold downward, like an umbrella closing, until all four are equally spaced in three dimensions.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] The three below fold downward, like an umbrella closing, until all four are equally spaced in three dimensions.

cues.text: A tetrahedron. In this simplified model, the repulsion found the arrangement on its own.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [short pause] [warmly] A tetrahedron. In this simplified model, the repulsion found the arrangement on its own.

cues.text: Here a simple computer model does the pushing: points on a sphere that repel, settling where the total repulsion is lowest.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Here a simple computer model does the pushing: points on a sphere that repel, settling where the total repulsion is lowest.

cues.text: This idea has a name: valence shell electron pair repulsion. VSEPR, for short.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [thoughtful] This idea has a name: valence shell electron pair repulsion. VSEPR, for short.

cues.text: Two regions, linear. Three, trigonal planar. Four, tetrahedral. Count the regions, and the arrangement follows.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Two regions, linear. Three, trigonal planar. Four, tetrahedral. Count the regions, and the arrangement follows.

cues.text: So the real skill is counting regions around the central atom. One counting rule makes it easy.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] So the real skill is counting regions around the central atom. One counting rule makes it easy.

cues.text: A single bond counts as one region.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] A single bond counts as one region.

cues.text: A double bond also counts as one. Its two shared pairs point the same way, between the same two atoms.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] A double bond also counts as one. Its two shared pairs point the same way, between the same two atoms.

cues.text: A triple bond? Still one region.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [curious] A triple bond? Still one region.

cues.text: And every lone pair on the central atom counts as one more region.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] And every lone pair on the central atom counts as one more region.

cues.text: Chemists write this as a short code. A is the central atom. Each X is a bonded atom. Each E is a lone pair.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [warmly] Chemists write this as a short code. A is the central atom. Each X is a bonded atom. Each E is a lone pair.

cues.text: Ammonia has three bonded hydrogens and one lone pair on nitrogen. A X three E.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Ammonia has three bonded hydrogens and one lone pair on nitrogen. A X three E.

cues.text: Add them up, three plus one, and you get four regions. That total is called the steric number.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Add them up, three plus one, and you get four regions. That total is called the steric number.

cues.text: And the steric number picks the arrangement.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [short pause] [thoughtful] And the steric number picks the arrangement.

cues.text: Let's put the rule to work, starting with carbon dioxide.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Let's put the rule to work, starting with carbon dioxide.

cues.text: Carbon makes two double bonds, one to each oxygen, and keeps no lone pairs. Two regions.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Carbon makes two double bonds, one to each oxygen, and keeps no lone pairs. Two regions.

cues.text: Two regions push to opposite sides, so the oxygens line up across the carbon. A X two. Linear.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Two regions push to opposite sides, so the oxygens line up across the carbon. A X two. Linear.

cues.text: Spin it any way you like. It stays a straight rod.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [warmly] Spin it any way you like. It stays a straight rod.

cues.text: Notice that each double bond holds four electrons, yet still acts as a single region. What matters is direction, not how many pairs share it.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Notice that each double bond holds four electrons, yet still acts as a single region. What matters is direction, not how many pairs share it.

cues.text: Next, boron trifluoride. Boron makes three bonds to fluorine and keeps no lone pairs. Three regions.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Next, boron trifluoride. Boron makes three bonds to fluorine and keeps no lone pairs. Three regions.

cues.text: Three regions spread around a circle. Every fluorine sits one hundred and twenty degrees from the next.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Three regions spread around a circle. Every fluorine sits one hundred and twenty degrees from the next.

cues.text: Tip it on its edge, and the whole molecule vanishes into a line. All four atoms lie in one plane.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [curious] Tip it on its edge, and the whole molecule vanishes into a line. All four atoms lie in one plane.

cues.text: A X three. Trigonal planar. Flat, like a three pointed star.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] A X three. Trigonal planar. Flat, like a three pointed star.

cues.text: Two regions make a line. Three make a flat triangle. But four regions cannot stay flat.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Two regions make a line. Three make a flat triangle. [short pause] [curious] But four regions cannot stay flat.

cues.text: Now methane. Carbon has four bonds and no lone pairs. Four regions. A X four.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Now methane. Carbon has four bonds and no lone pairs. Four regions. A X four.

cues.text: The flat guess puts them in a square, ninety degrees apart.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] The flat guess puts them in a square, ninety degrees apart.

cues.text: But in a square, every region has two neighbours crowding it at ninety degrees. There is room to do better.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] But in a square, every region has two neighbours crowding it at ninety degrees. There is room to do better.

cues.text: Let the regions use the third dimension. Two tilt up, two tilt down, and every gap opens wider.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [warmly] Let the regions use the third dimension. Two tilt up, two tilt down, and every gap opens wider.

cues.text: Now every region is the same distance from every other. That is the tetrahedron.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Now every region is the same distance from every other. That is the tetrahedron.

cues.text: Put hydrogens at the four tips, and you have methane. Every angle between two bonds is the same.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Put hydrogens at the four tips, and you have methane. Every angle between two bonds is the same.

cues.text: Where does that number come from? Place the carbon at the centre of a cube.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [curious] Where does that number come from? Place the carbon at the centre of a cube.

cues.text: The four hydrogens sit on alternate corners of the cube, as far apart as they can get.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] The four hydrogens sit on alternate corners of the cube, as far apart as they can get.

cues.text: Two bond directions are then one, one, one, and one, minus one, minus one.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Two bond directions are then one, one, one, and one, minus one, minus one.

cues.text: Their dot product is minus one, and each has length root three.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Their dot product is minus one, and each has length root three.

cues.text: So the cosine of the angle between them is minus one third.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] So the cosine of the angle between them is minus one third.

cues.text: Take the inverse cosine, and out comes one hundred and nine point four seven degrees.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Take the inverse cosine, and out comes one hundred and nine point four seven degrees.

cues.text: Not a number to memorise. Just the geometry of four equal directions.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [short pause] [warmly] Not a number to memorise. Just the geometry of four equal directions.

cues.text: Now for the most important idea in this story. Start again with methane's four regions.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [thoughtful] Now for the most important idea in this story. Start again with methane's four regions.

cues.text: Swap the carbon for nitrogen. Nitrogen has five valence electrons. Three go into bonds with hydrogen.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Swap the carbon for nitrogen. Nitrogen has five valence electrons. Three go into bonds with hydrogen.

cues.text: The other two stay home, as a lone pair on the nitrogen.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] The other two stay home, as a lone pair on the nitrogen.

cues.text: A lone pair is still a region of electron density. It still takes up space, and it still pushes.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] A lone pair is still a region of electron density. It still takes up space, and it still pushes.

cues.text: So ammonia still has four regions: three bonds and one lone pair. A X three E. The four have an approximately tetrahedral arrangement.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] So ammonia still has four regions: three bonds and one lone pair. A X three E. The four have an approximately tetrahedral arrangement.

cues.text: But here is the catch. When we describe a molecule's shape, we only look at where the atoms are.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [curious] But here is the catch. When we describe a molecule's shape, we only look at where the atoms are.

cues.text: Hide the lone pair, and look at the atoms alone.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Hide the lone pair, and look at the atoms alone.

cues.text: Nitrogen at the top, three hydrogens below. A pyramid with a triangular base. Trigonal pyramidal.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Nitrogen at the top, three hydrogens below. A pyramid with a triangular base. Trigonal pyramidal.

cues.text: So there are two descriptions. The electron geometry includes every region, lone pairs too. For ammonia, that is tetrahedral.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] So there are two descriptions. The electron geometry includes every region, lone pairs too. For ammonia, that is tetrahedral.

cues.text: The molecular geometry includes only the atoms. For ammonia, that is trigonal pyramidal.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] The molecular geometry includes only the atoms. For ammonia, that is trigonal pyramidal.

cues.text: The lone pair is invisible in the final shape. But it decided the shape.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [short pause] [thoughtful] The lone pair is invisible in the final shape. But it decided the shape.

cues.text: And there is one more effect. Measure the angle between two hydrogens. It is not one hundred and nine point five.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] And there is one more effect. Measure the angle between two hydrogens. It is not one hundred and nine point five.

cues.text: It is about one hundred and seven degrees. The bonds are squeezed slightly closer together.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] It is about one hundred and seven degrees. The bonds are squeezed slightly closer together.

cues.text: A lone pair is held by only one nucleus, so in the VSEPR picture it spreads out close to the nitrogen, and crowds the bonds.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] A lone pair is held by only one nucleus, so in the VSEPR picture it spreads out close to the nitrogen, and crowds the bonds.

cues.text: Now replace one more hydrogen with a lone pair. The central atom becomes oxygen, with six valence electrons.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Now replace one more hydrogen with a lone pair. The central atom becomes oxygen, with six valence electrons.

cues.text: Two of them bond with hydrogens. The other four form two lone pairs.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Two of them bond with hydrogens. The other four form two lone pairs.

cues.text: Count the regions: two bonds, two lone pairs. Four again. A X two E two.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Count the regions: two bonds, two lone pairs. Four again. A X two E two.

cues.text: So the electron geometry is still tetrahedral. The four-region arrangement is approximately tetrahedral.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] So the electron geometry is still tetrahedral. The four-region arrangement is approximately tetrahedral.

cues.text: Now hide the lone pairs.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Now hide the lone pairs.

cues.text: What's left is an oxygen and two hydrogens, joined at an angle. Water is bent.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] What's left is an oxygen and two hydrogens, joined at an angle. Water is bent.

cues.text: And the angle? About one hundred and four point five degrees. Smaller again.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] And the angle? About one hundred and four point five degrees. Smaller again.

cues.text: Two lone pairs crowd the bonds more than one did, so the angle closes a little further.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Two lone pairs crowd the bonds more than one did, so the angle closes a little further.

cues.text: Put the three side by side. Methane, no lone pairs, one hundred and nine point five.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Put the three side by side. Methane, no lone pairs, one hundred and nine point five.

cues.text: Ammonia, one lone pair, about one hundred and seven.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Ammonia, one lone pair, about one hundred and seven.

cues.text: Water, two lone pairs, about one hundred and four point five.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Water, two lone pairs, about one hundred and four point five.

cues.text: Same four regions, same tetrahedral electron geometry, three different molecular shapes.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Same four regions, same tetrahedral electron geometry, three different molecular shapes.

cues.text: A word of honesty, though. VSEPR is a qualitative model. For methane, ammonia and water, it explains the decreasing angles.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [thoughtful] A word of honesty, though. VSEPR is a qualitative model. For methane, ammonia and water, it explains the decreasing angles.

cues.text: The exact numbers are measured, and they depend on the atoms involved and on the full electronic structure.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] The exact numbers are measured, and they depend on the atoms involved and on the full electronic structure.

cues.text: There is no simple formula that turns lone pairs into degrees.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] There is no simple formula that turns lone pairs into degrees.

cues.text: Now look back at our opening mystery. Water's oxygen has four regions, two of them invisible lone pairs.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [warmly] Now look back at our opening mystery. Water's oxygen has four regions, two of them invisible lone pairs.

cues.text: Carbon dioxide's carbon has just two regions, two double bonds, and no lone pairs.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Carbon dioxide's carbon has just two regions, two double bonds, and no lone pairs.

cues.text: Water has four regions, but only two bonded atoms. Carbon has two regions. Their different electron arrangements solve our mystery.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [short pause] [warmly] Water has four regions, but only two bonded atoms. Carbon has two regions. Their different electron arrangements solve our mystery.

cues.text: And the same counting works for bigger molecules too.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] And the same counting works for bigger molecules too.

cues.text: What happens with five regions? Five points can't all be equally spaced on a sphere.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [curious] What happens with five regions? Five points can't all be equally spaced on a sphere.

cues.text: Start from the tetrahedron and add a fifth region at the bottom. Watch them settle.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Start from the tetrahedron and add a fifth region at the bottom. Watch them settle.

cues.text: Three regions spread around the middle, in a flat triangle. These are the equatorial positions.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Three regions spread around the middle, in a flat triangle. These are the equatorial positions.

cues.text: The other two sit straight above and below. The axial positions.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] The other two sit straight above and below. The axial positions.

cues.text: Two pyramids joined at their base: a trigonal bipyramid.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Two pyramids joined at their base: a trigonal bipyramid.

cues.text: Unlike the tetrahedron, its angles are not all equal.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Unlike the tetrahedron, its angles are not all equal.

cues.text: Equatorial to equatorial, one hundred and twenty degrees.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Equatorial to equatorial, one hundred and twenty degrees.

cues.text: Axial to equatorial, ninety degrees.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Axial to equatorial, ninety degrees.

cues.text: And axial to axial, straight through, one hundred and eighty.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] And axial to axial, straight through, one hundred and eighty.

cues.text: That difference between the positions will matter in a moment.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [thoughtful] That difference between the positions will matter in a moment.

cues.text: Phosphorus pentachloride, in the gas phase, has exactly this shape. Five chlorines, five bonds, no lone pairs. A X five.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Phosphorus pentachloride, in the gas phase, has exactly this shape. Five chlorines, five bonds, no lone pairs. A X five.

cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Its axial bonds are even a little longer than its equatorial ones. The two kinds of position are not equivalent.

cues.text: So when lone pairs appear, where do they go?

cues.text: Replace one region with a lone pair. There are two kinds of place it could go.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Replace one region with a lone pair. There are two kinds of place it could go.

cues.text: Put it in an axial spot, and it has three neighbours only ninety degrees away.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Put it in an axial spot, and it has three neighbours only ninety degrees away.

cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Put it on the equator, and only two neighbours are that close. The others are a roomy one hundred and twenty degrees away.

cues.text: Ninety degree contacts are the most crowded, so the lone pair takes the equator.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] [thoughtful] Ninety degree contacts are the most crowded, so the lone pair takes the equator.

cues.text: That's sulfur tetrafluoride. Four bonds, one lone pair. A X four E.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] That's sulfur tetrafluoride. Four bonds, one lone pair. A X four E.

cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Hide the lone pair, and the atoms make a seesaw. The lone pair even nudges the bonds slightly away.

cues.text: Look at the whole family. The same five region arrangement every time.
cues.tagged_text: [warm, conversational delivery] Look at the whole family. The same five region arrangement every time.
